K341,256 and buliding regulation K170,553.92
Management and Support Services program has been allocated a total of K 4.9 million to facilitate for
the smooth operations of the institution. An allocation of K2.6 million will go towards human resources
and administration to cater for general operations of the Local Authority (LA). Executive management
has an allocation of K642,419 to provide an oversight role at the LA. Audit has an allocation of K432,500
to ensure that internal controls in the institution are upheld. Procurement has an allocation of K407,722
to ensure that procurement of goods and services is done according to set laws and regulations. ICT has
been allocated K402,850 to cater for software installation and to ensure that ICT policies are adhered to.
Accounting management has been allocated an amount of K211,592 to cater for dismatling of debt owed
to various institutions and individuals. The allocation will further enhance proper inventory of all Council
property. Lastly Public Relation has been allocated an amount of K168,145 to cater for information
dissemination and publication of the progress and happenings at the LA in order to bring the information
to the general public.
Resource Mobilsation programme has been allocated a total amount of K2.2 million which will be
channelled towards the procurement of two motorbikes for revenue collection especially in the outskirts
of the district, construction of checkpoint houses and construction of a parking bay at Munada area and
construction of a fence around North Luangwa lodge to enhance security. It will also cover salaries for all
accounting staff
District Health Services which is yet another devolved function has been allocted an amount of K5.3
million translating into K4.6 million for primary health services and K666,891 for district health
coordination. This will enhance health service provision in the district.
Veterinary Services has been allocated an amount of K137,101 to ensure animal health in the district is
improved and also reduce animal disease prevelance. This too is a devoved programme.
Lastly, Transport Services Programme has been allocateed an amount of K3.7 million to cater for road
maintanance in the district.

Table 6 shows the programme output of the Constituency Development Fund (CDF). Under the Community
projects component, the LA has budgeted to procure two ambulances for the two constituencies of Chama
district for the District Health Office (DHO). The LA has also planned to procure seven (7) motorbikes for the
Chief returners for all the seven Chiefdoms in Chama district. Further, the LA has budgeted to procure
approximately 5000 more desks for Chama North which still has a desk deficit which was not planned for in
the previous year (2023). It should also be noted that that the LA, has included desks for all the new Class
Room Blocks (CRBs) constructions to be undertaken in 2024. Two maternity wings will be constructed in
Pondo, Chipala ward and at Chibale Rural Health Centre (RHC) in Nkhankha ward. In addition, two
reticulation systems will be installed within the district, one at the main police post, Kamphemba ward and
another one at Kambili Health Post (HP) in Mphalausenga ward. It should be noted that the district especially
for Chama South has received massive support from the World Vision projects who have been drilling
boreholes, installing water reticulation systems and constructing ablution blocks at all public institution in six
(6) wards of Chama South. Fifty (50) boreholes out of which twenty-eight (28) are water reticulation systems
have been drilled. World Vision has finished feasibility studies in six (6) more ward of Chama North and
Chama South and has indicated that they will provide water in the same ward. World Vison has further
indicated that they will be in the district for fifteen (15) years.
Further, the LA has planned to disburse 100 percent of the CDF loan and grant funds to organised groups
within the district. The turnout of applications for the empowerment component has been massive and the
LA has had no challenges in disbursing the funds. However, in terms of implementation, some of the
beneficiary of the grant component have not utilised the fund as intended. Currently the implementation
rate is at 54% and the LA authority intends to increase that to atleast 70% with more field monitoring and
evaluation for the year 2024.
Furthermore, the LA has planned to increase the number of pupils under the CDF bursaries component from
the 418 to 568 pupils in 2024. For skills development, the LA plans to increase the number of sponsorships
from 57 to 300 students in 2024. The current numbers of students are low due to the low interest levels by
the youth within the district to apply for skills development programmes as initially perceived. However,
after inviting Chipata trades institution within the district to conduct fasttracked processing of acceptance
letters for students, a good number of students showed up and applied for the sponsorship to be considered
in 2024. The LA will continue to sensitize and invite other reputable TEVETA accredited institutions within the
district to offer fasttracked processing of acceptance letters as it appears youths cannot afford to get
acceptance letters for skills courses outside the district.
Lastly, under the CDF administrative component, the LA plans to conduct ten (10) CDFC meetings to facilitate
for CDF project approvals, Support the WDCs technically through backstopping their meetings and providing
them with stationery for them to conduct their meetings. Equipment such as two (2) laptops, two (2)
printers and an ICT server to support e-GP procurement among other automation services at the LA.

socio-economically sound and environmentally sustainable district by 2040 for the
sole purpose of poverty reduction.
I would like to express special gratitude to His Excellence, the President of the
Republic of Zambia Mr. Hakainde Hichilema for the support by allowing us to use
part of the administrative component under CDF for the formation of the
Integrated Development Plan (IDP). This in itself is one of the indicators that he has
continuously shown to ensure that the district becomes a prosperous district by
2030 through social and economic empowerment of all the sectors of
development.
We are more than delighted as a district to be beneficiaries of the support
rendered in Eastern Province by USAID Local Impact Governance Project, World

Project (TRALARD) during the Preparation of this important document.

Councilors, the District Commissioner and the Heads of Government
Departments, the Council Secretary and the entire IDP team for working diligently
in the preparation of the district Integrated Development Plan which will be used
as a tool to improve the livelihoods of the community. In addition, I wish to thank

all seven traditional leaders for playing an active role in the development of this
document.

governance structure: central government, local government and traditional

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Chama District Integrated Development Plan (IDP) outlines a strategic vision
for sustainable development over the next decade, aiming to guide the district’s
development toward an interlinked, socio-economically sound and
environmentally sustainable district by 2045. As prescribed by Urban and Regional
Planning Act, Chama District’s IDP is comprised of planning survey and issues
report, a development framework, an implementation programme, a report on
public consultation, as well as appropriate diagrams and plans.
As the foundation of the document, the planning survey and issues report
comprises of the description of Chama as a district; it speaks to matters of the
district’s demographic status, settlement patterns, land use, and various impact
assessments. In addition, this component includes sector-based thematic
analyses that help depict the district’s performance and current development
status. It brings out the issues relating to the implementation of national policies
and programmes, accessibility, availability, and quality of services provided in the
district. Additionally, it also covers issues to do with environmental impacts and
social aspects of the communities across the district. It is on this foundation that
the development framework is developed.
Based on the planning survey and issues report, the development framework is
basically the remedies to the challenges faced by the district; This component
defines the district’s goals, objectives and strategies. Following a similar structure,
the development framework presents these goals and objectives in a thematic
sector-based format outlining the different types of challenges faced. This is then
concluded with a summary of cross-sectoral goals, objectives, strategies, and
programmes to be implemented over the prescribed planning period.
Furthermore, the gathered information becomes part of the key ingredient that
v
speaks to the depiction of spatial development on the ground in the spatial
development framework. Subsequently, the spatial development framework
becomes the platform for financial allocation or in other words, the
implementation programme.
The implementation programme helps define the roles and responsibilities of all
stakeholders both internal and external to the district; In this component, the
document covers the capital investment programme, the local authority’s
financial plan, and lastly the monitoring and evaluation plan.
Ultimately, the IDP is the collective composition of these components brought to
life by the synergetic efforts of all stakeholders in the district. It is my sincere desire
to witness the actualization of the district’s vision for a better Chama district come

PART ONE – INTRODUCTION
Introduction and Background
The Chama Integrated Development Plan is a comprehensive framework guiding
the socio-economic transformation of the rural district. Located in the heart of
Eastern Province, Chama district is endowed with fertile soils and favorable
climate conditions, making agriculture the backbone of the local economy. Rain-
fed agriculture, in particular, plays a vital role in the livelihoods of residents, with
maize such as rice, cotton, maize, groundnuts and beans being the primary
source of income. As the largest district in Eastern Province, Chama boasts an
unparalleled natural heritage, with a significant portion of its terrain comprising
the pristine wilderness of the Upper Luangwa Valley. This strategic location,
adjacent to the renowned North Luangwa National Park, presents both
opportunities and challenges for sustainable development.
The opportunities and challenges include the following;
1. Tourism potential: Upper Luangwa Valley’s unique biodiversity and wildlife
populations offer significant tourism potential.
2. Job creation: Tourism and conservation efforts create employment
opportunities for local communities.
3. Conservation benefits: The Game Management Area help protect
biodiversity, maintaining ecological balance and preserving natural
resources.
4. Revenue sharing: Communities can benefit from revenue sharing schemes
with tourism operators and conservation organizations.
5. Cultural preservation: GMAs can promote cultural heritage and traditional
practices related to wildlife management and opportunities for
community-based tourism initiatives, promoting cultural exchange and
local economic benefits.
6. Research and education: GMAs can serve as outdoor laboratories for
research, education, and skills development.
7. Community-based natural resource management (CBNRM): Empowers
local communities to manage natural resources, promoting sustainable
livelihoods.
However, the district faces significant development challenges. The poor road
network, exacerbated by the rainy season, severely limits accessibility to most
parts of the district, hindering economic growth and service delivery. The district’s
rugged terrain and limited infrastructure hinder access to markets, social services,
and economic opportunities.
Other challenges related to Chama being located in a GMA include the
following;
1. Human-wildlife conflict: Competition for resources, space, and livelihoods
lead to conflicts between humans and wildlife.
2. Limited land use: GMA has imposed restrictions on land use, potentially
limiting agricultural expansion and development.
3. Security concerns: Poaching, habitat destruction, and human safety
concerns require significant resources and effort.
4. Economic benefits distribution: Ensuring fair distribution of benefits among
local communities, tourism operators, and conservation organizations.
5. Climate change: Impacts on wildlife populations, habitats, and ecosystem
balance.
6. Policy and legislative frameworks: Complexities in laws, regulations, and
policies governing GMAs are too rigid.
To address these challenges and unlock the district’s potential, this IDP prioritizes:
1. Agricultural development and diversification
2. Infrastructure development (roads, storage facilities, and market access)
3. Environmental conservation and sustainable natural resource
management
4. Improved access to social services (health, education, and water)
5. Enhanced economic opportunities through value addition and
entrepreneurship
6. Promote citizen participation in local governance
7. Foster partnerships and collaborations among stakeholders to drive
development
Through this IDP, we envision an interlinked, socio-economically sound and
environmentally sustainable Chama District, where residents enjoy improved
livelihoods and the natural resources are harnessed for the benefit of all.
Definition of the IDP Area
The proposed IDP Area for the Chama shall cover the whole District as narrated
in the Chama District boundary as defined in the Provincial and District Boundaries
Act Cap 286 of the Laws of Zambia.
District location map
Chama is one of the 15 districts in Eastern Province of the Republic of Zambia. The
largest district in Zambia's Eastern Province, Chama District, has its headquarters
located at Chama, Kamphemba ward. It encompasses a sizable wilderness
situated in the Upper Luangwa valley, northeast of the North Luangwa National
Park. It is composed of the Chama North and Chama South constituencies. It is
situated between longitudes 31.450 and 32.300 East and latitudes 13.800 and
14.450 South with altitudes from 350 m to 640 m above sea level and the
escarpment rises to 1,200 m above sea level.
The district stretches between latitudes 100 15’ to 120 10’ South and longitude 320
40’ to 330 10’ East. Chama is a transit town, linking Eastern Province and Malawi
to Muchinga, Northern and Luapula Provinces. The district’s town Centre is
located about 940 KM away from the Capital City of Zambia (Lusaka), about 332
KM away from the Provincial Headquarters Chipata, about 450 KM away from
Nakonde the border town and about 156 KM away from Lundazi.
Chama District is surrounded by six (6) Districts and an international boundary on
its Eastern part where it shares a long stretch of border with Malawi, on the
Northern part Chama District shares its border with Mafinga, Isoka and Chinsali
Districts, on its western part Chama boarders Shiwang’andu District and Mpika
District on the South-Western part while on its Southern part the district shares its
border with Chasefu District.
The notable features in the district include, Muchinga Escarpment in the East,
Nyika Plateau in Mbazi Ward, Hot springs dotted around the district, the North
Luangwa National Park, and Luangwa River that passes across the district. Figure

Climatic Condition
The district lies in Agro-ecological Region II, which is characterized by low rainfall.
The rainfall pattern is controlled by the movements of the Inter-Tropical
Convergence Zone and increases from south to north. Therefore, the district is
characterized by the tropical continental type of climate with three distinct
seasons, i.e., hot rainy season from late November to April; a cool-dry season, from
May-August; and a hot - dry season, from September to early November. The
mean annual rainfall is in the range of 700 - 900 mm. The district often experiences
frequent drought and floods.

Hydrology
The Luangwa River that flows north to south longitudinally cuts the district almost
into two equal halves and has the following tributaries; Luumbu, Kalinkhu,
Mbwata, Kamphemba in the north and Bazimu, Lupamazi, Lunzi, Luelo, Luvila and
Lundazi in the south. Most of them dry up in the dry season living isolated pools of
water along river-beds.
Vegetation
There are three (3) main types of predominant vegetation under Chama District
namely; (a) Mopani woodlands, which are infertile and found on poor sandy
loam soil; (b) Miombo woodlands, found on hilly highlands with moderate fertile
soils and (c) Munga, locally known as Musangu usually found on fertile alluvial soils
where human settlements are mostly concentrated. However, it is worth to note
that there are also minor occurrences constituting watersheds and small patches
of palm communities and traces of grass land found along the river banks and
surrounding areas.
The district has four (4) gazzetted National forests and 1 local forest covering a
total area of 333, 566 Hectares. These include; Lundazi, Makutu, Chire, Fibale, and
Pondo Forest respectively. Customary Land has a large portion of open forest
whose size is not yet known. However, a large portion of the district is a valley
where the Luangwa North National Park is situated.
Flora and Fauna
The district is predominantly covered by three vegetation types, the Mopane
woodlands, the Miombo woodlands and the Munga. However there exists a
mosaic of vegetation types on the valley floor constituting of Riparian, Montane,
Munga and Itigi. Other vegetation types in the district include riverine, shrublands,
grasslands and riverine vegetation. The riverine vegetation found along the rivers,
streams and lagoons and dambos usually have a mixture of such as Faidaherbia
albida, pilistigma thorniigii (musekese), and Acasia species. There are also
patches of palm communities.
Jachmann et al (1994) and Jachmann (1998) have established that Luangwa
valley contains some of the highest densities of larger mammals in Zambia. A total
of 110 mammal species exist that include seven species near endemic to the
area. These include: elephants, eland, hippos, buffalo, zebra, waterbuck, roan,
bushbuck, bushpig, warthog, kudu, puku, impala, grysbok, oribi, common duiker;
lion, leopard, spotted hyena, wild dog, greater kudu, sable antelope; among the
primates: baboon, vervet monkey, night ape and bush baby. Other fauna
includes birds, reptiles, fish and invertebrates.
Governance and General Administration
Chama District has three tier governance systems namely; Traditional, Local
Government and Central Government (district administration) which all
coordinate and propagate district development and general welfare of the
people. However, all these governance structures are streamlined through
various policies and guidelines to operate in an integrated approach for the
common good of national development.
Traditional Leadership System
Chama District has seven (7) Chiefs namely; Senior Chief Kambombo, Chief
Lundu, Chief Chibale, Chief Chikwa, Chief Tembwe, Chief Chifunda and Chief
Mulilo who are responsible for enforcing customary law through various
committees of advisers and village headmen. The main inhabitants of the district
are the Senga speaking people. The district also boasts of the Bemba and
Namwanga speaking people who are found in the northern part of Chama, and
Tumbuka speaking people on the southern part.
Local Government System
Chama Town Council is responsible for the Local Government administration
system. The Council was established in 1900s after the abolishment of Rural
Councils following an integrated Local Administration Act of 1980 that saw the
establishment of all District Councils in the Country. Furthermore, in 2012 Chama
District was realigned to Muchinga province from Eastern Province after the
creation of Muchinga Province under the Patriotic Front administration.
Administratively, Chama District was taken back to Eastern Province under the
United Party for National Development in 2021. Chama district has two (2)
constituencies named Chama North which is demarcated into thirteen (13)
administrative Wards and Chama South Constituency with eleven (11) wards, with
each Ward coordinated by an Area Councilor who is elected every 5 five years
in accordance with the Local Government electoral system in Zambia.
The total twenty-four (24) Ward Councilors constitute a Council headed by the
Council Chairperson forming the district legislative structure responsible for;
overseeing Programmes and projects in the district, making by – laws,
administering the district and performing other prescribed functions. The Council
is supported by management headed by the Council Secretary who is supported
by technical and administrative personnel responsible for general administration
and policy interpretation and implementation.
The twenty-four (24) wards are subdivided into 91 zones with each ward having a
sub-district governance structure called Ward Development Committee (WDC)
which acts as a link between local communities and the Local Authority (LA). The
WDCs are non-political and members are democratically elected by the
community. These are headed by Chairpersons who are assisted by executive
members and zonal representatives. This decentralized and democratized level
of governance has been facilitating high level of consultation and active
participation of local people in the development process in the district. Like other
constituencies Chama North and Chama South Constituencies’ developmental
aspirations are represented by two area Member of Parliaments (MPs) in the
Legislature arm of governance at national level.
District Administration
The District Administration is headed by the District Commissioner who co-
ordinates Central Government functions and all developmental activities as well
as harmonizing functions with those of local authorities and other line ministries in
order to ensure effective implementation of developmental Programmes in the
district. The District Commissioner is supported by Heads of Government
Departments from various line Ministries and sectors who report directly or through
quarterly District Development Coordinating Committee (DDCC) meetings.

contemporary agricultural skills, entrepreneurial abilities, professional career
achievement, etc. To put it another way, individuals lack the skills necessary to
find work, and urban investment activities are unable to accommodate them. In
light of this, it is necessary to proactively prepare for the majority of people living
in rural areas so that they may actively participate in and sustainably lead local
economies.

Disability Status
Effective development implementation is based on inclusive planning, which is

Median Age
The median age of a population is the age at which it is split into two numerically
equal groups, meaning that half of it is under the age and the other half is above
it. A median age that is lower than 20 years shows a young population; that which
is between 20 and 30 years indicates an intermediate population that is either
becoming younger or ageing; while a population with a median age above 30
years is an old population (SOURCE). The 2022 census statistics shows the median
age for the district at 18 years, implying that Chama district has a young
population. This implies that there is a large workforce potential: Majority of
population is entering or already in working age; Economic growth potential:
Young population can drive economic expansion; Innovation and
entrepreneurship: Young people can bring new ideas and energy; Adaptability:
Young populations can adapt quickly to changing technologies. However, this
calls for meeting educational needs of a young population, creating jobs for a
growing workforce, addressing health needs of adolescents and young adults,
and providing support for youth, including mental health and recreation.
Age Dependency Ratio
Age Dependency Ratio is the ratio of the population aged 0-14 years and persons
aged 65 years and older, per 100 persons of working age 15-64 years. It shows the
burden of dependency on the productive population. The 2022 projected census
statistics shows that the district has an overall age dependency ratio of 114.9
translating from the child dependency ratio of 107.4 and age dependency ratio
of 7.4 per 100 persons of working age 15-64 years. These statistics shows a high
ratio indicates more dependents per working-age individual, high Child
Dependency Ratio indicates a large proportion of children dependent on
working-age individuals, and the relatively low Old-Age Dependency Ratio
suggests fewer elderly dependents. This suggests that there is need to plan for
more social service facilities. Economically, this indicates an increased tax burden
on working-age group, pressure on social security and pension systems, potential
labor market strain due to high youth population, and opportunities for economic
growth through youth entrepreneurship and innovation.
Migration and Urbanization
Similar to other districts, Chama has seen a rise in migration as a result of
commerce, education, and job. The primary driver of migration, particularly
among young people, is unemployment. There aren't any significant industries or
large corporations in Chama area to take in the vast amount of jobless youths.
Because of this, the majority of young people travel to new places like Lundazi in
quest of employment and a better living. The government is the largest employer

Population projections are crucial because they aid in making plans for the future
well-being of human communities. In terms of size and composition by age and
sex, population projections can give a general idea of the most fundamental
aspects of future human societies (CSO, 2013). Cohort component technique
and mathematical models are the two fundamental approaches used to create
population projections (CSO, 2013). The most accurate way to predict the
population is to use the cohort component model, which accounts for all the
factors that influence population change, including net migration, death, and
fertility. The cohort component technique is thought to be the best standard for
population predictions, although it is less helpful at lower administrative levels
when demographic change data may be absent or incorrect. Therefore,
forecasts at the national level are typically made using the cohort technique.
Using a mathematical table is acceptable for population prediction at the sub-
national level (CSO, 2013).

Impact of the Continuation of Population Growth on Land Use and Spatial
Development Patterns
Population growth has profound effects on land use and population distribution,
presenting both opportunities and challenges. Population growth can drive
economic development by expanding the labor force and consumer market.
Urbanization, fueled by population growth, can foster innovation, cultural
diversity, and improved infrastructure. Increased population demands better
transportation, services, and amenities, contributing to overall economic growth.
However, population growth also poses significant challenges. Land
degradation, resulting from increased pressure, leads to deforestation, soil
erosion, and habitat loss. Unplanned urban growth results in sprawl, congestion,
and decreased quality of life. Resource scarcity, environmental degradation, and
climate change are additional concerns.
It is expected that with the trend in the existing population, there will be
agricultural expansion, driven by food demand that will contribute to
deforestation and habitat loss. Further, urbanization is anticipated that will convert
natural areas and agricultural land to urban uses, while infrastructure
development will fragment habitats. These changes will have far-reaching
consequences for ecosystems and biodiversity.
In terms of population distribution changes, it is anticipated that urbanization will
lead to increased density and strain on services. Migration patterns will shift as
people will seek better opportunities. Changes in population demographics, such
as age and sex structure, will influence land use and resource demands. In
addition, the district has started experiencing urban population growth around
Kamphemba Ward.
To address these challenges, there will be need for sustainable urban planning,
resource-efficient technologies, conservation and restoration efforts, education
and family planning, and infrastructure development (public transportation,
green spaces) will be essential.

Assessment of the Existing State of Development
The assessment of Chama District's commerce and trade sector reveals that

entrepreneurship and expand local businesses. Additionally, access to financial

Availability of Services Relevant to this Sector
The economy of Chama is primarily driven by subsistence agriculture and local
trade, with a limited range of supporting infrastructure, including retail
establishments, financial services, and hospitality facilities. The district's remote
location and underdeveloped status hinder the growth of economic activity,
constraining the potential for market expansion and diversification.
Markets
Chama District has a single gazetted market located in Kamphemba Ward, while
five other markets (Tembwe, Chikwa Chibale, Kanyelele, Kambombo, and
another) remain ungazetted. The district also features several growth nodes,
including Kaozi, Muyombe Turnoff, Lundu, Katangalika, Mulilo Kalovya,
Chifunda, and Mapamba.
Banking Facilities
Chama District has limited banking services, with only one non-commercial bank,
NATSAVE, operating in the area. However, several other financial service
providers are available, including GS salary advance, Totten gram financial
services, ZOONA, Zanaco agents, and mobile money services such as Airtel
Money, Zamkwacha, and MTN Money.
Trade
The trading activities in Chama are dominated by small-scale entrepreneurs
engaged in various retail businesses, including hardware, building materials,
groceries, and foodstuffs such as rice, fish, maize, and vegetables. These
commercial activities are concentrated in the Central Business District (CBD) and
growth centres throughout the district.
Cooperatives
Chama District has approximately 540 cooperatives engaged in various
economic activities, primarily maize cultivation and trading. The district has
benefited from the Presidential Solar Hammer Milling Initiative, with 9 solar milling
plants allocated, 65% of which are operational. The initiative is implemented by
the Zambia Cooperative Federation, with support from the Department of
Cooperatives and Entrepreneurship. Additionally, banking institutions provide
loans and mortgages to promote business growth, with 80 cooperatives among
those that have received funding.
Gas Service Stations
As of 2024, Chama district faces a significant challenge in accessing fuel, with no
operational gas service stations within its boundaries. Consequently, residents are
forced to procure fuel from neighboring Lundazi district. Furthermore, the local
market is plagued by illegal fuel vendors, exacerbating the situation. Despite
interest from prospective investors to establish a gas station in Chama, the poor
state of the road network has hindered the transportation of fuel, thereby
deterring investment in this critical infrastructure. Addressing the road network
challenges is essential to attracting investment and improving access to fuel
in the district.
Issues from Public Participation Process
Chama district faces several challenges hindering its economic growth. Key issues
from the public engagement included inadequate markets and trading spaces,
insufficient storage and processing facilities for rice production, high commodity
prices due to poor road networks, limited banking services in rural areas except
for Kamphemba ward, face challenges in accessing financial services, hindering
their ability to benefit from government initiatives such as CDF grants and loans,
and poor network connectivity.
Several wards in Chama District face network challenges that hinder access to
financial mobile banking services. In Chama South, affected wards include
Mapamba, Chilenje, Lunzi, Chipala, Vilimukulu, and Lumezi. Meanwhile, in
Chama North, areas with network difficulties comprise parts of Muchinga,
Mazonde, Nkhankha, Luangwa, Chisunga, and Ndunda. These connectivity
issues pose significant obstacles to the efficient use of mobile banking services in
these districts.
Impact of Changes Anticipated Over the Next Ten Years
Chama district faces a significant challenge in meeting the minimum requirement
of having at least one market per ward. Currently, only Kamphemba ward has an
officially recognized market, leaving a shortfall of 23 markets. To address this,
market infrastructure development is underway, including the construction of the
Tembwe Market shelter in Mabinga Ward and the Chibale Market shelter
in Nkhankha Ward.

HOUSING SECTOR
The housing sector in the district involves construction, development, and
management, purchasing, selling, and renting of property, engaging
stakeholders such as developers, government entities, NGOs, and companies.
The focus will include implementing priorities from the 8th National Development
Plan (8NDP), National Housing Policy, and District Implementation Plan along with
assessing environmental impacts of current developments on climate change,
gender-related issues, and external factors affecting the sector.
Key Government Priorities to Be Implemented at A Local Level
Chama district is currently facing a housing crisis as there is limited good standard
housing infrastructure for local residents as well as government departments and
institutions providing various services to the district. As a result, this has affected
the quality of life and service provision; Impacts such as floods and natural
disasters in both Chama North and Chama South constituencies have further
amplified this issue (Vilimukulu and Lunzi ward floods in 2019, Heavy rainfall and
winds in Lundu Chiefdom in 2024 among others). Ripple effects of these impacts
affected the social wellbeing of victims during these trying times.
As a response to this issue, the government at district level has prioritized the
increase of access to affordable and standardized housing units as well as
improving the security of land tenure for different social groups; As a road map,
the 8NDP and National Housing Policy will guide the district’s action toward
addressing this issue. The stated priorities are to be actualized through
government interventions such as the land development fund, construction of
housing units for public facilities through means such as the CDF, establishment of
planning agreements, and housing programmes supported by non-
governmental organizations. In addition, these interventions are collaborative
and will involve the collective effort of all government departments and relevant
stakeholders within and beyond the district during the planning period.
The expected outcome is a reduction in housing deficiency, mitigation of housing
related social issues, improved resilience to climatic impacts and disasters, and
enhanced land tenure security for district residents as well as both public and
private institutions.
Description of the existing state of development
The following section looks at the state of development of the housing sector in
Chama district, the key performance indicators, and how the district is performing
at the current moment.
Availability of services
As one of the basic human rights, housing is a priority of the government and a
service to be appreciated by the public. As it stands, only 2273 households in
Kamphemba ward which is 8% are within planned state land and can acquire

WATER AND SANITATION SECTOR
The Water and Sanitation sector is responsible for development and
management of water resources, provision of clean water supply and adequate
sanitation in the district. This sector provides a review on existing plans and
strategies that govern the performance and highlights the core issues affecting
sector development in the district.
Key Government Priorities to Be Implemented at a Local Level
The Chama district faces significant challenges due to inadequate clean water
supply and underdeveloped sanitation infrastructure. These issues lead to disease
outbreaks, environmental degradation, poor economic growth, and food
insecurity. Residents often rely on shallow wells and pit latrines, increasing the risk
of waterborne infections, especially during floods.
To address these problems, Chama has outlined two main priorities aligned with
national development plans: enhancing water resource management through
increased investments and improving access to clean water and sanitation.
Efforts will include establishing water points, constructing dams, developing water
schemes, installing hand pumps, and promoting community awareness on
sanitation practices. Implementing these strategies aims to improve public health,
sanitation, and the overall economic conditions in the district.
Description of the existing state of development
The overall performance of water and sanitation sector in the district can be
described as below average. It is below the set target of 90% both for water
supply and sanitation.
Urban Water Supply
Public water supply and sanitation are essential for socio-economic
development. The Eastern Water and Sanitation Company Limited (ESWC)
provide piped water in urban and peri-urban areas, servicing 1,080 customers
and 188 households through three kiosks. However, 10,998 households in these
areas rely on boreholes and do not receive piped water from ESWC. Areas lacking
access to piped water include Chimwemwe, Makeni A and B, Mtayachalo
compound, Hospital Area, Magroceries, Kazenga, Chizimba, parts of Lukombozi,
and sections of East Rise. This urban network is as shown in Figure 6.

140,326. However, 66 boreholes are non-functional, contributing to water access
challenges. The distribution of boreholes is uneven, with Kamphemba, Mwalala,
Lumezi, Lupamazi, and Kalinkhu wards having a higher concentration of water

The Local Authority, in collaboration with partners like World Vision Zambia,

through the CDF to improve water supply. In 2022, World Vision Zambia drilled 17

Urban Sanitation
Chama District lacks a public sewerage system, and most households rely on
onsite treatment methods like septic tanks and soak ways for waste

facilities for temporary disposal by traders and residents. With the urban
population growing, there is a pressing need for investment in sanitation
infrastructure to enhance sanitation for individual homes.
Rural Sanitation
In order to enhance sanitation levels in the rural areas, the Local Authority in

only Lundu Chiefdom has been certified as Open Defecation Free (Map 8).

Issues arising from public participation process
The situation in Chama District is dire, with most areas lacking access to clean
water and sanitation services. Even where these services are available, they're
often inadequate. This is particularly concerning in public institutions like schools
and health facilities. For instance, out of 160 schools, only 8 have waterborne
toilets, and 79 schools have access to clean water. More than 60% of health
facilities in the district also lack these essential services. However, with the
enhanced Constituency Development Funds (CDF) and other interventions,
there's hope for improvement. The government's efforts to address these
challenges, such as the construction of dams and boreholes, are crucial steps
towards ensuring access to clean water and sanitation services for all
Impact of Changes Anticipated Over the Next Ten Years
One of the given and fundamental anticipated changes over the next ten years
is population growth. Based on the calculated population projection, Chama
district is to reach a population of 194,072 by 2035. This will place a demand for
an additional water point, the extension of the current water supply network, and
the establishment of functional sanitation facilities and infrastructure across the
district. Furthermore, there is a need to consider significant investment in parallel
infrastructure development to cope with the anticipated need for water supply
in other sectors such as agriculture, industrial, and health among others.
Future Demand for Services and Facilities Based on the Estimates of Population
Change
The increase in Population in the next ten (10) years based on the district’s
calculation indicates a growth of up to 194,072 residents at a growth rate of 2.5%.
This entails that the district should plan for supply of water to 38,814 households
across the district. Based on the analysis of the current water point coverage, 136
additional water points are needed to adequately supply the current population
at 140,784 (28,157 households) and approximately 837 water points for population
at 2035 (Chama district, 2024). Sanitation services will need to be supplied to the
projected population across the district.
Impact of Ongoing Development Programmes on Land Use and Population
Distribution Patterns
The ongoing construction of water schemes and boreholes in Chikwa, Chifunda,
and Chama North aims to enhance water access in the district, while the ODF
(Open Defecation Free) program in Chama South is set to improve health and
hygiene. Despite these efforts, there is a lack of strategic investment in sanitation
infrastructure, leading to substandard stayaways and septic tanks, as well as
numerous pit latrines and shallow wells that could compromise water quality.
Population patterns are expected to remain consistent, with urban areas and
rural zones near water sources experiencing continued growth, potentially
resulting in encroachment on sensitive areas like the Kamphemba river buffer
zone and groundwater well fields due to land shortages.
Impact of Environment and Climate Change
Implementing projects such as Dam construction poses several environmental
challenges including Habitat Destruction. Dams can flood large areas of land,
resulting into destruction of natural habitats for various species of plants and
animals, Agricultural fields and infrastructure. Prior to construction, a lot of trees
maybe cut down during and after construction of the Dam. This can lead to loss
of biodiversity and disrupt ecological balance.
Primitive practice trends such as Open Defecation will significantly affect the
preservation of the environment for future generations because groundwater
may be contaminated.
Addressing these challenges requires careful planning, comprehensive
Environmental Impact Assessments, and implementation of Mitigation measures
such as habitat restoration efforts. Engaging with the local communities and
stakeholders throughout the planning and implementation process will be
essential.
Issues Arising Relating to Gender Groups and Vulnerable Groups
In Chama District, traditional roles place a heavy burden on women and girls for
household chores like fetching water, often requiring long, exhausting journeys.
This affects girls' education, as they spend substantial time gathering water
instead of attending school. Boys are also affected, as they often assist with water
collection, impacting their schooling and well-being.
Youth, the largest demographic, face inadequate water and sanitation
infrastructure, although existing facilities are generally inclusive. The elderly and
disabled encounter access challenges at hand-pump water points, experiencing
discrimination and limited hygiene access. Women and vulnerable groups also
lack awareness about cross-cutting issues like HIV/AIDS, with some falling victim to
exploitative situations involving contractors on water projects.
Addressing these issues demands infrastructure improvements, better sanitation,
and gender equality efforts.
External Factors Contributing to the Issue
The major external factor contributing to these issues is inadequate investment in
the water and sanitation sector and erratic funding of programmes in the water
sector. The lack of spatial analysis in the distribution of water points has
contributed to the identified issue. This had caused biased drilling and installation
of boreholes in the rural parts of the district. There are other notable factors
contributing to the issues such as unplanned settlement under housing sector
affecting issues of water and sanitation. Attaining Open defecation free (ODF)
status has been an issue in rural areas due to noncompliance of community
members and lack of support from Traditional leaders as major external factors.
Lack of crossing points in the district has also led to inadequate water and
sanitation facilities in the district.
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTRY SECTOR
Forestry and Natural Resources sector is mandated to oversee, conserve, and
preserve natural resources and protect the environment. Forests and Natural
Resources are central to the achievement of a low carbon green economy and
sustainable development. The following chapter looks into the environment and
forest sector; Insights of this sector include governmental plans, priorities, and
policies implemented at district level including analyses of the district’s
performance and issues raised by residents.
Key Government Priorities to Be Implemented at A Local Level
As one of the unique districts located in a game management area with a
gazetted national forest, Chama faces a threat of environmental degradation
which is the core issue of the environment and forestry sector. Loss of biodiversity
and forest cover poses threat to the tourism industry, compromises resilience to
floods and droughts, and affects good economic growth among other factors.
In order to address this issue, the government at district level has identified two
key priorities; Government intends to regulate and monitor the exploitation of
forest resources and industrial activities in the district and increase forest
hectarage under community forest management. Through collaborative efforts
among government departments and other organizations, the district will
facilitate the regeneration of forest areas, facilitate the establishment of
community forest management areas, regulate and monitor the exploitation of
forest resources, and enforce environmental regulations.

Availability of services
The forestry department executes a number of functions as prescribed under the
Forestry Act 2015; Functions of the Forestry department include;
1. To Identify and demarcate forest areas to be protected as National Forests,
Local Forests, Botanical Reserves, Community forests and Joint Forest
Management Areas.
2. Control, manage, conserve and administer Protected Forest Areas.
3. Promote methods for sustainable utilization, conservation and
preservation of ecosystems and
biological diversity in non- protected forest areas.
4. Develop and implement strategies for reducing emissions from
deforestation and forest degradation to address impacts of climate
change through mitigation and adaptation measures.
5. Establish and manage local and regional supply forest plantations.
6. Promote and provide technical support for private sector participation in
the development of forest plantations, timber industry, beekeeping and
non-wood forest products.
7. Conduct research on forestry and related matters.
8. Maintain a forest information management system.
In order to carry out these functions, the forestry department extends its services
through a network of forest camps; the department has 5 forest camps namely
Kalovya, Makutu, Chire, Fibale, and Pondo.
Forest camps in strategic areas lack officers due to insufficient housing, hindering
effective environmental management and resource monitoring. The forest
department relies on partnerships with other district stakeholders to perform its
functions, which are restricted to shared interests with other government bodies,
such as law enforcement. Consequently, most communities, except those near
Kamphemba ward, have no local forest department officer presence.
Quality of services
From the functions stated in above, the district’s department has endeavored to
provide quality services to the residents and stakeholders. Through collaborative
efforts, the department makes amends for some of the lacked administrative
capacity deficits such as limited manpower and financial resources. This has
helped particularly with provision of services such as issuance of permits,
facilitation for concession licenses, community capacity building, and others such
as establishment of plantations and nurseries. Though as it stands, the district does
not have an established plantation.
Other functions are based on the mandate to regulate the exploitation of natural
resources, this involves monitoring and inspection patrols in the gazzetted national
forest as well as community forests. Similar to the previously stated functions,
limitations include a lack of human and financial resources as well as other
necessities namely monitoring vehicles, and camp staff houses among others.
Issues Arising from Community and Stakeholder Consultations
Stakeholder engagement revealed several challenges faced by communities
and stakeholders. These include the lack of affordable alternative energy sources
to replace or supplement the widespread use of wood and charcoal fuel.
Additionally, the high cost of establishing individual alternative energy systems is
especially burdensome in rural areas. The absence of forestry officers in forest
camps also hinders timely access to services for natural resource exploitation and
the acquisition of licenses and permits, particularly for residents in remote areas.
Although carbon trading is seen as a positive development in the district, many
residents struggle to embrace it due to the limited immediate benefits.
Impact of Changes Anticipated Over the Next Ten Years
Population growth intensifies the demand for forest products, such as timber,
fuelwood, and charcoal, impacting the environment significantly. This increase in
demand leads to deforestation, which disrupts the hydrological cycle and
biodiversity, especially as forested land is converted for agriculture near water
bodies. The forestry sector faces added strain from increased resource extraction,
necessitating more patrols, infrastructure, and staffing to protect natural resources
and combat illegal activities. Additionally, poverty exacerbates environmental
degradation, as population growth amplifies pressure on natural resources,
further stressing conservation efforts.
Impact of Ongoing Development Programmes on Land Use and Population
Distribution Patterns
Land use change is arguably the most pervasive socioeconomic force driving
changes and degradation of ecosystems. This trend will cause loss of soil fertility,
loss of biodiversity, soil erosion, siltation, climate change, global warming, water
and air pollution, vegetation loss, topography destruction, water table
destruction and recharge zones will be affected. Population distribution pattern
might cause high encroachment in protected forest reserves due to shortage of
land and loss of soil fertility (shifting cultivation).
The department and other stakeholders have to work with other sectors to ensure
that the right land use is achieved as well as making sure that no plots or land is
falling in any protected forest area. It is also imperative that the planners,
agriculture officers and forest officers see to it that adherence in terms observing
farms are 50m away from streams and rivers.
Impact of Environment and Climate Change
Global climate change, driven mainly by greenhouse gas emissions, is causing
rising temperatures and altering weather patterns, leading to more extreme
weather events. Mining expansion, increased timber concessions, and
unsustainable farming practices are further depleting forest resources, disrupting
the hydrological cycle, and exacerbating climate impacts. These activities
threaten conserved lands and accelerate resource depletion.
Forestry departments are tasked with revenue generation, ecosystem
preservation, and biodiversity conservation. Revenue from wood and non-wood
forest products, which supports rural livelihoods and provides alternative income
sources, is at risk if canopy cover decreases, negatively impacting beekeeping
and other forest-dependent activities. Reduced forest cover also diminishes
carbon sequestration, which may alter temperatures and rainfall patterns. The
department’s primary focus is on sustainable natural resource management to
protect these resources for future generations.
Issues Arising Relating to Gender Groups and Vulnerable Groups
Efforts in community forest management (CFM) promote gender equity, with 30%
of women participating in decision-making. This inclusion reduces social and
economic hardships for women, who rely heavily on forest resources like
fuelwood, mushrooms, and other non-timber products. Deforestation poses a
unique challenge for women, increasing their travel distances and decreasing
resource availability, thus affecting livelihoods.
In beekeeping, cultural beliefs often exclude women, though they show high
dedication in forest management. Support for women’s beekeeping initiatives
through training and resources are underway. Men’s engagement in traditionally
female forest activities could enhance income generation for communities.
Youth involvement in environmental programs is encouraged to instill sustainable
practices. For persons with disabilities, environmental barriers restrict participation,
and climate change disproportionately impacts them, heightening risks like HIV
transmission during climate-related migrations.
External Factors Contributing to The Issue
Human activities like mining, industrialization, deforestation, and unsustainable
farming are significantly impacting the environment by disrupting water tables,
recharge zones, and ecosystems. This leads to disturbances in the hydrological
cycle, contributes to climate change, and causes biodiversity loss. Over time,
such disturbances may cause a shift in forest species composition, known as
succession, potentially eliminating endemic species.
Climate Change and Environmental Sustainability
The district's environmental sustainability assessment focuses on the pivotal issue
of environmental degradation, encompassing deforestation, threats to wildlife
habitats, detrimental practices, and population growth. A comprehensive
approach is employed, presenting interventions to address the core issue,
alongside analyses of anticipated changes, public concerns, and external factors
exacerbating environmental degradation.
Key Government Priorities to Be Implemented at A Local Level
The threat of environmental degradation was prompted proactive action from
the government at district level. As such, the government has prioritized the
promotion of sufficient sustainable mitigation and adaptation initiatives as well as
increase access to alternative energy sources to combat climate change and
enhance environmental protection. Collaborative effort will be made to secure
water sources, regulate the exploitation of natural resources, reinforce
environmental regulations, and promote relocation of settlements from flood
prone areas.
Description of the existing state of development and key performance indicators
The Urban and Regional Planning Regulations of 2020, under the Urban and
Regional Planning Act of 2015, support development control through land use
regulations for various purposes (housing, commercial, agricultural, industrial). This
control incorporates environmental protection and climate change
considerations for obtaining development permissions. Effective control,
however, is primarily enforceable on state land (e.g., part of Kamphemba ward),
with planning agreements proposed for customary land administration.
Water management in Chama is supported by the 2022–2026 Strategic Plan
involving stakeholders like Chama Town Council, EWSC, and UNICEF. Activities
include aquifer mapping and water point improvements. The district aims for
green energy transitions via solar power plants in Lundu and Kambombo
chiefdoms, but efforts require expansion for comprehensive energy sustainability.
Forest conservation is mandated by the National Forestry Act, promoting
Community Forest Management Areas (CFMAs). Chama has 1 national and 4
local forests with 17 CFMGs aiding forest protection. The Game Management Plan
(GMP) aligns with local Community Resource Boards (CRBs), managed by chiefs,
to oversee wildlife habitat conservation across five chiefdoms.
Climate-smart agriculture covers 12,000 hectares, promoting sustainable farming
to mitigate environmental impact. In an effort to mitigate climatic impacts such
as floods, the district has mapped flood prone areas as depicted in Figure 17 and
through the Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit (DMMU), has provided aid
and relief interventions to such areas. The challenge is that settlements have
developed and keep developing in flood prone areas because communities
know that they will receive food from government. Therefore, there is need for a
robust resettlement plan for such areas.
Availability of services
The summary of development control and related efforts in Chama District
highlights several key challenges and initiatives. Chama District faces significant
difficulties in enforcing development control, particularly in areas of customary
land, which constitute over 90% of its territory. This challenge is exacerbated by
unregulated local land uses that pose environmental threats. Areas covered at
present are those with planned state land in Kamphemba ward while measures
to cover the remaining areas in the 24 wards are being developed.
To mitigate these environmental degradation and climatic impact issues, various
initiatives have been devised. Environmental initiatives include utilizing the
Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to establish tree nurseries and ensuring
that contractors replant trees cleared during construction. Additionally, the URP
planning regulations of 2020 require that all developments reserve at least 20% of
their area for greenery.
In terms of water and sanitation, efforts are being made to map and secure
aquifer areas while promoting District Water and Sanitation Health Education
(DWASHE). At current, only Kamphemba area has a mapped-out water aquifer.
There are also plans for solar power plants in Lundu and Kambombo chiefdoms
to enhance renewable energy sources.
Forest management is supported by the presence of the existing national and
local forests and 17 Community Forest Management Groups (CFMGs).

Issues from Public Participation Process
The stakeholder engagement in Chama District revealed public concerns that,
while not directly linked to environmental protection, impact the effectiveness of
existing initiatives. Mitigation measures focus on reducing environmentally harmful
practices and promoting alternative livelihoods, facilitated by community groups
like CRBs and cooperatives. However, challenges persist, including unequal
benefit distribution, uneven workloads, and a preference for immediate returns
over long-term programs like carbon trading. Other issues include non-
compliance among members, retention of traditional farming methods due to
difficulty adopting new practices, and insufficient technical support.
Various environmental programs are implemented district-wide, though not all
reach every area. Key initiatives include development control, water resource
management, wildlife conservation, and forest management. Programs such as
TRALARD and carbon harvesting aim to promote resilience, but some remain in
early phases or face logistical challenges. Solar energy projects are yet to be
established, while flood response and food security programs are more reactive.
Overall, while there is growing recognition of the importance of environmental
protection, enhanced support, training, and adoption of alternative energy
solutions are needed to boost effectiveness.
Impact of Changes Anticipated Over the Next Ten Years
Arising from the projection of population growth, it is anticipated that should the
current development trends persist, there will be a more rapid loss of forest cover
especially in areas where livelihood activities heavily depend on forest resources.
Areas experiencing the pressure of development are the major growth nodes
(Chibale, Lundu, Kalinkhu, Kambombo, Chikwa, and Chifunda). This is attributed
to the sparse location trend of settlements that are distant from one to another in
areas like Lundu, Chikwa and Chifunda hence the need for reinforcement of
stakeholder engagements and implementation of environmentally sustainable
economic alternative livelihood activities. Areas like Kalinkhu, Kambombo, and
Chibale on the other hand, have a nucleated settlement pattern and as a result,
this places a demand for environmental protection due to increase in population
and economic activity.
Impact of Environment and Climate Change
As observed from past events, the Chama district has been at the receiving end
of natural disasters induced by climate change; The 2019, 2021, 2022, and 2024
floods in both North and South Constituencies are examples of how climate
change has affected the district. While climate change may be a global
phenomenon, a closer investigation shows that the Chama district had a role to
play in the magnitude of the impacts. Agricultural activity in areas such as
riverbanks weakened the river borders. This coupled with the clearing of land
increased the extent of the damage caused by the floods.
Additionally, the increase in population also places a demand for wood fuel
which directly links to the depletion of natural forest resources. With the
anticipated growth in the next ten years, the district will face more dire
consequences should such trends be left unchecked. Consequences may
include;
✓ Migration of wildlife from past animal corridors
✓ Further devastation of public infrastructure
✓ Collapse of fragile local area marketing networks
Issues Arising Relating to Gender Groups and Vulnerable Groups
Climate change exacerbates environmental degradation and social
vulnerabilities in Chama District, disproportionately affecting women, girls, youths,
differently-abled individuals, and those living with HIV/AIDS. Women and girls face
displacement, domestic burdens, gender-based violence, and limited decision-
making power, while men and boys encounter health hazards and human-wildlife
conflicts. Youths are vulnerable to environmental and economic challenges,
leading to poverty and job scarcity. Despite these challenges, Chama District is
actively working towards gender balance, climate resilience, and inclusive
development, promoting equal opportunities, social equity, and economic
participation for all, including differently-abled individuals and those
living with HIV/AIDS.
External Factors Contributing to the Issue
Global climate change has far-reaching implications, and consequently,
economic activities beyond Chama District's borders that generate substantial
greenhouse gas emissions constitute an external factor influencing the district's
environmental sustainability.

The quality of service of the existing mines and exploration mines are below

Impact of Changes Anticipated Over the Next Ten Years
The mining sector creates opportunities for employment, an increase to the
sustenance to local and also a national treasury. It has been noted that overall,
Chama has received proposals to establish mines from individuals and firms
obtaining prospecting licenses which is even more likely to increase. Within the
next ten years, it can be anticipated that the district may have more than two
mining firms operating. Nevertheless, the impacts anticipated also pose
detrimental effects to various social groups and the environment.

Impact of Environment and Climate Change
The mining sector is highly energy-intensive, contributing significantly to
greenhouse gas emissions. Carbon dioxide emissions vary depending on the type
of resource mined and the mining processes used. Environmentally, mining leads
to hillside erosion, deforestation, pollution, and biodiversity loss. Many exploratory
mines are situated in remote, flood-prone areas, making access difficult,
especially during extreme weather events. Unpredictable weather, especially
flooding, often halts mineral production as site access for investors becomes
limited.
Issues Arising Relating to Gender Groups and Vulnerable Groups
Mining in Chama district is predominantly male-dominated due to perceptions
that mining requires intensive labour, limiting female participation. Youths, aged
18-35, are the most active demographic in both legal and illegal mining activities.
Although most roles are filled by men, one environmental mining project is
managed by a woman, highlighting the need for more gender sensitivity to
promote equity. The district has only illegal mines, and women are typically
involved in non-mining roles, such as meal preparation.

Description of the Existing State of Development and key performance indicator
Despite having certain tourist attractions, such as Nyika Plateau National Park,
which is located in Zambia's Chama District in the Eastern region and spans an
area of around 80 square kilometers, the district has not seen many tourism-
related activities. In 1972, Nyika was designated as a national park. Along the
international border, Nyika Plateau National Park has a shared boundary with
Malawi Nyika National Park. The highest altitude park in Zambia's national park
system is Nyika, which ranges from 1,295 to 2225 meters above sea level.
In terms of vegetation, The Nyika Plateau National Park is a strikingly a beautiful
park of montane grassland and relict forest patches. The common small animal
fauna includes the four striped grass rat, the black and red squirrel, the two-
spotted palm civet and three species of swamp rat. The larger mammals include
Maloney’s monkey, klipspringer, reedbuck, bushbuck, blue duiker, zebra, roan
antelope, eland and leopard. Bird-watching is excellent all year round at Nyika
Plateau National Park but best between October and January, when migrant
birds are present. The common birds include secretary bird, auger buzzard, green
loerie, white-neck raven, black-eyed bulbul, common stone chart, African
boubou, fiscal shrike, common waxbill.
The district has a rare and natural wood fossilization and palaeontology site at
Sitwe (Figure 8) located 38.9km from Chama CBD and it covers an area of about
100 meters in radius that is believed to have existed for over 150 million years.
However, the site is not protected making it vulnerable to human disturbance and
the local people do not know the importance of a fossil land or area.

The district hosts a magnificent traditional ceremony known as Kwenje. The main
goal of the ceremony is to educate and raise awareness among Zambians about
the "Sound of the Kwenje" drums, which proclaim danger, coronation, and
funerals. Various dances, including the male-dominated Visangu/Gogo dances
and the Chidiwiti dance for both sexes, are performed throughout the event. The
ceremony, marked by a wild party atmosphere complete with drums and
whistles, is held in the Chiefdom of Kambombo.
The district's hospitality sector comprises 16 lodges and guest houses, although
none meet the standards of a full-fledged hotel. While these establishments cater
to local and regional visitors, they fall short of accommodating international
tourists' expectations. However, during hunting season, the district experiences an
influx of tourists, primarily served by a limited number of hunting camps, notably
Kanusha and Nutoboze.
The district is home to two significant Iron Stone Age sites, Mutemba Libwe and
Njunga, which hold immense tourism potential due to their rich iron smelting
materials, including bog iron, Haematite stone, and ancient furnace ruins. These
sites offer a unique glimpse into the region's cultural and industrial heritage, but
lack essential amenities to fully develop as tourist destinations, presenting an
opportunity for infrastructure development and preservation efforts to unlock their
potential.
The district is home to two revered royal burial sites: Kambombo and Mulilo. The
Kambombo site, with a rich history spanning over 200 years, serves as the final
resting place of Chief Zamangwe. These sacred sites host seasonal rituals, paying
homage to the spirits of deceased chiefs and seeking blessings of good health,
prosperity, and success for the chiefdom. The rituals foster peace, reverence, and
unity among the community, emphasizing the importance of honouring their
heritage and leadership. However, there is need to secure these sites and
improve them in order for them to become attractive visiting sites. Map 13 shows

TRANSPORTATION AND COMMUNICATION SECTOR
The sector is comprised of transport and communication infrastructures which
include telecommunication, roads and storm-water drainage. A well-established
transport system enables efficiency in transporting goods and services and overall
cost of conducting business.
Key Government Priorities to Be Implemented At a Local Level
The sector is currently using the National Transport Policy of 2019. The policy
endeavors to promote development of road transport services, facilities and
infrastructure that meet the global safety standards through construction,
maintenance, upgrading, and rehabilitation, thereby promoting sustainable
mobility of both goods and passengers to achieve economic and social needs,
and develop systems to facilitate Non-Motorized Transport.
The Eighth National Development Plan prioritizes at improving the road network
infrastructure and improve Information Communication and Technology (ICT)
infrastructure for quality service delivery. These strategies are to be implemented
at local level through the construction of and maintenance township and feeder
roads, installation and construction of culverts and bridges, installation of mast
towers, and improvement of the local community radio station for efficient
transportation and communications, construction and maintenance of a bus
station, establishment of a new taxi rank, construction of a filling stations and
develop systems to facilitate non-motorized transport in the district.
Status of Implementation of Existing Plans
The district has 5 major roads leading into and out of the district namely; Chama-
Matumbo Road, Chama-Lundazi Road, Tembwe Road, Muyombe Road, and
Chama-Chibale Road. The municipality has a large and well-maintained street
network with a drainage system. These township Roads have street lights installed,
making the streets safe and secure and improve on the business hours. Chama
Town Council plays a major role in the maintenance of the township roads.
Additionally, the district lacks a modern bus station which can house all the public
transport.
The district's rural areas are connected via a network of poor, often impassable,
gravel and earth roads. The majority of roads require maintenance, including the
construction of crossing points and bridges, which are often nonexistent. Under
road development and maintenance, the Local Authority in collaboration with
Road Development Agency conduct routine works for vegetation control along
the Chama-Matumbo Road and Chama-Lundazi Road. The local authority has
deliberately procured earth moving equipment using CDF to enhance the
maintenance and development of access and feeder roads.
In terms of air transport, the district has three small airfields which can only
accommodate small aircrafts, however, only two (2) and functional and they lack
essential infrastructure. The Luangwa River passes through the district and it is used
as another mode of transport to connect Chipala and Lunzi Wards.

domestic and foreign travelers. The tourist potential of Chama in North Luangwa
National Park is considerable.
The communities where growth will occur include; Chama CBD, Tembwe Centre,
Kambombo Centre, Chifunda Centre, Mulilo Centre, Lundu Centre and Chikwa
Centre as well as areas along the two main roads and around water points. These
areas will require more services such as access roads and mobile communication
network. With the construction of the Chama-Mutombo and Chama-Lundazi

Impact of Environment and Climate Change
Road transportation may have an adverse effect on climate change and the
environment. Fossil fuels, the primary energy source for Chama's automobiles,
trucks, and buses, contribute to the release of greenhouse gases, a primary cause
of climate change. Degradation of air quality is another possible adverse
environmental effect of vehicle mobility. Additionally, the district's roadways,
which are primarily made of gravel, are in poor condition and emit a lot of dust,
which pollutes the air.
On the other hand, road infrastructure is impacted by climate change. Soil
erosion and floods in the galleries are caused in part by the absence of drainage
systems. These pose a risk to human health and the environment. In order to make
the road network climate change robust, climate change interventions like
culverts and drainage systems are required.
Issues Arising Relating to Gender Groups and Vulnerable Groups
Most road infrastructures lack bridges and drainage, which makes them
susceptible to deterioration. During the rainy season, gullies and potholes form on
the surfaces of the roadways. As a result, vulnerable populations—such as
women, people with disabilities, and children—are unable to access institutions
like healthcare facilities and schools.
Furthermore, women farmers are similarly impacted as the inadequate road
system limits their ability to move about and produce. The roads in the district are
not user friendly to PWD, thus, there is need to ensure that road infrastructure
accommodate the needs of People With Disability.
External Factors Contributing to the Issue

Charcoal consumption in the district is alarming, projected to double by 2030,

increased from 34% to 51% in urban and rural areas. However, this growth comes

investments to mitigate these consequences.

Deforestation, land degradation, and habitat loss, leading to biodiversity decline
and ecosystem disruption. Burning wood and charcoal releases greenhouse
gases, contributing to climate change, air pollution, and health issues.

sequestration, exacerbating global warming.

The health sector aims to provide accessible, affordable, and quality healthcare
services to families in Chama District, while also promoting a healthy environment.
This section reviews existing plans and strategies, and identifies key challenges
hindering sector development in the district.
Key Government Priorities to Be Implemented at a Local Level
Prevention of disease is a key aspect in effective public health management. The
district places priority on more effective investments in primary healthcare by
strengthening fundamental components of the health systems aimed at
promoting and maintaining a clean, healthy environment and good nutrition in
order to prevent diseases.
Key Priorities of the Development Plan, Policies, Strategies and how they are to be
implements at a Local Level
The key priorities outlined in the 8NDP for the sector include reducing disease
burden, maternal and infant mortality and increase life expectancy. This was
designed to be implemented in the district through provision of quality and
effective healthcare services by promoting hygiene, improved nutrition, health
education, increased coverage of occupational health and ensure equity of
access to quality, cost-effective and affordable maternal and child health
services.
The key strategies outlined in the NHS plan of 2022 focuses on addressing the
health sector challenges and accelerating progress towards attainment of the
national and global health goals, aimed at ensuring equitable access to quality
healthcare to all in Zambia, as close to the family as possible, while leaving No
One Behind. The district focuses on the equitable deployment and distribution of
staff, provision of suitable accommodation for staff and construction of new
health facilities.
Assessment of the Existing State of Development
Chama has one first level referral hospital and forty-three rural health facilities.
These include two Zonal health centers, eighteen health centers and twenty-
three health posts as shown in Map 17 below.
Patients are still faced with a challenge of distances to access medical services
from the nearest health facility. The picture is that most of the patients cover a
walking distance of more than 15 km especially those in the remote rural areas.
Malaria incidence continues to rise in the district. Some of the interventions
include Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS), routine distribution of ITNs, case
management and health promotion to eliminate malaria in the district. The target
still remains to reduce the incidence of malaria from 571/1,000 to 271/1,000 by the
year 2026. Diarrhea incidence in under five increased from 165.5/1000 in 2020 to
187/1000 in 2023 (Chama District Health Office, 2023). Coverage on Cesarean
section reduced from 8% in 2022 to 7% in 2023 (Chama District Health Office,
2023). 3rd ANC coverage reduced to 19.7% from 21.3% in 2021 (Chama District
Health Office, 2021).
The sector has a total of 77 houses against a target of 129 houses of which many
of these houses are in a poor condition. Hence the need for adequate
accommodation in all the health facilities to offset this housing deficit.
Only two facilities connected to piped water are on national electricity grid. The
rest of the facilities are dependent on solar power which needs urgent
maintenance.
Transport still remains a challenge in the district with high maintenance costs due
to bad terrain. Only 28 health facilities have running motorbikes. There is need to
urgently address transport challenges for easy referral and service delivery.

Impact of Environment and Climate Change
Climate change -related weather events strain healthcare staff, disrupt physical
infrastructures; interrupt supply chains making it difficult to treat patients and
threatening healthcare quality and safety.
The establishment of health facilities in Chama District is a commendable
initiative; however, the incinerators installed at these facilities pose a significant
environmental concern. The emission of greenhouse gases from these incinerators
contributes to climate change, which is anticipated to exacerbate the morbidity
and mortality rates associated with climate-sensitive diseases.
Malaria, being the most prevalent disease in Chama District, necessitates
continuous monitoring due to the district's propensity for flash floods. The perennial
flooding creates stagnant water pools, providing ideal breeding environments for
mosquitoes that transmit malaria. Consequently, it is essential to prioritize
measures that mitigate the environmental impact of health facilities while
ensuring the district's preparedness to address the challenges posed
by climate change.
