Key Government Priorities to Be Implemented at A Local Level
In promoting social well-being and development across the district, the
government is focusing on integrating vulnerable and marginalized groups into
development initiatives and enhancing access to social welfare services. These
efforts aim to alleviate poverty and foster conditions conducive to economic
growth. In line with this, Chama district has been rolling out several key programs.
Aligned with the goals of the Eighth National Development Plan (8NDP), the
district prioritizes reducing poverty, vulnerability, and inequality while
strengthening its policy and governance frameworks. Programs such as the Food
Security Pack (FSP), Supporting Women’s Livelihoods, Women’s Empowerment,
and Social Cash Transfers use registered beneficiary data, while initiatives like Self-
help, Adult Literacy, Early Child Marriage prevention, and Family Reintegration
are case-specific.
In terms of national policies, the district implements the National Policy on
Disability, supporting the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities. This policy strives to make the country more inclusive for people with
disabilities, with Chama district also acting. Efforts include inclusive infrastructure
designs for health facilities, schools, and markets, incorporating features like
ramps to improve accessibility.
Assessment of the Existing State of Development
Statutory services focus on legislative aspects, particularly regarding child
welfare, and include the Day Nurseries Act, CAP 313, the Adoption Act, CAP 54,
the Maintenance Orders Act, CAP 55, the Juveniles Act, CAP 54, and the
Probation of Offenders Act, CAP 93 of Zambia.
(a) Court Investigations
Social Welfare Officers, designated as Child Welfare Inspectors, conduct
investigations on behalf of the courts to provide recommendations that support
fair and beneficial outcomes for juvenile offenders. The department handles 6 to
10 court investigation cases per quarter.
(b) Probation of Offenders
Probation involves either institutional or community-based rehabilitation for
juveniles in conflict with the law, supervised by a Probation Officer under the
Probation of Offenders Act, CAP 93. This constitutional duty of the Department of
Social Welfare aims to guide juveniles towards responsible citizenship through
intensive counseling. The department typically manages at least 10 juvenile
probation cases.
Non-Statutory Services
Non-statutory services include social assistance programs like the Public Welfare
Assistance Scheme (PWAS), Drought Emergency Social Cash Transfer (D-ECT),
and Social Cash Transfer (SCT), aimed at poverty alleviation in local communities.
(a) Public Welfare Assistance Scheme
PWAS focuses on providing necessary goods and services, not cash, to vulnerable
groups, including the incapacitated and terminally ill. Due to limited funding, the
support provided is often insufficient.
(b) Drought Emergency Social Cash Transfer (D-ECT)
This government initiative assists households affected by drought during the
2021/2022 and 2023/2024 farming seasons. It includes both vertical expansion
(increased support for existing SCT beneficiaries) and horizontal expansion
(support for new households affected by disasters). Chama currently has 5,389 D-
ECT beneficiaries, totaling 7,105 since the first phase in 2023.
(c) Social Cash Transfer (SCT)
The SCT program provides bimonthly cash support to vulnerable households,
aiming to reduce extreme poverty and prevent its transmission to future
generations. Households with disabled members receive double the standard
transfer, amounting to K800, while others receive K400. In Chama, 8,139
households benefit from SCT, and some have used their funds to invest in livestock
and housing, thereby building assets and improving their quality of life.
Supporting Women’s Livelihood (Grievance Redress Mechanism, Village
Banking): The Supporting Women’s Livelihoods (SWL) programmes to beneficiaries
include, context-specific training, mentoring and peer support, the provision of
productivity grants, and facilitation of savings groups.
Chama is one of the districts in Zambia implementing the GEWEL project. The
district has three (3) sub-centre staff and 119 community-based volunteers (CBVs)
who are trained and are now helping to run the project at community level.

Impact of Environment and Climate Change
The district has recognized several key growth areas in response to the observed
population increase and economic expansion. Major growth nodes include
Chibale, Lundu, Kalinkhu, Kambombo, Chikwa, and Chifunda, while secondary
growth nodes are Kanyelele, Katangalika, Tembwe, Kalovya, Chasato, Manga,
and Kalasa. Investments in infrastructure, such as roads, schools, and healthcare
facilities, are expected to drive economic activity, promote urbanization, and
cause a shift in population centers toward newly developed zones. Improved
social protection programs may improve living conditions, encouraging rural-to-
urban migration in search of better opportunities and services. This shift is likely to
lead to a change in land use, moving from traditional agriculture to a broader
mix of residential and commercial developments. These transitions will also affect
the allocation of resources and services, influencing both demographic trends
and spatial planning within the district.
The impacts include shifts in temperature and rainfall patterns, which influence
crop yields and the overall availability of food. Additionally, climate-related
displacement leads to migration and social upheaval. In flood-prone areas,
floods can also damage critical infrastructure within affected communities.
Issues Arising Relating to Gender Groups and Vulnerable Groups
The program helps women, girls, boys, men, vulnerable individuals, and those
living with HIV/AIDS, as long as they fulfill the selection criteria, with no issues.
External Factors Contributing to The Issue
The district’s role in handling caseloads is limited because the Ministry of
Community Development and Social Services determines the number of cases it
oversees. Similarly, the district lacks decision-making power regarding the funding
it receives for its programs, making it reliant on external allocations to carry out its
initiatives.
Furthermore, the district’s ability to influence the effectiveness of its programs is
impacted by the capacity of other organizations involved in areas like Child
Justice and early marriage prevention. Since these partners operate
independently, the district cannot fully manage or direct their contributions.
When it comes to community beliefs and practices, the district does not have
direct authority to enforce cultural changes. Instead, it relies on awareness
initiatives and educational programs, such as those aimed at teaching young
men about responsible adulthood. These efforts serve to gradually influence
attitudes within the community, fostering a shift toward more positive societal
norms.

The vision for Chama District
With the perspective of the future at hand, Chama district’s long-term vision is:
“An interlinked, socio-economically sound and environmentally sustainable
district by 2045”
Mission statement for Chama district
To enhance socio-economic development through facilitating an interlinked
transport network, infrastructural development, social well-being, and diversified
economy in a sustainable manner.
Key aspects of the vision
Chama district crafted its vision for the next ten years through reflexivity or self-
reflection; the district took into consideration;
Interlinkages - Chama District's strategic location, bordering six districts and one
international border, presents vast trade opportunities. However, inadequate
transportation and communication infrastructure has hindered regional and
international trade growth. To overcome this, the district aims to develop an
integrated transport and communication network that will unlock potential in
agriculture, tourism, and other sectors.
Socio-economically sound - The vision seeks to create a prosperous district where
economic growth and social well-being coexist. This will be achieved through
fostering a vibrant economy, reducing poverty and inequality, promoting
entrepreneurship and innovation, collaborations and partnerships, and ensuring
access to quality services.
Environmental sustainability - Chama District's natural riches are threatened by
unsustainable practices. Chama will shift to eco-friendly lifestyles and renewable
energy sources, like solar power, that will protect the environment and secure a
sustainable future.
Ultimately, it is the combined synergy or unified function of these factors that will
bring Chama district’s vision to life.
Planning Values for the Chama District IDP
As a basis to realize this vision, Chama district has identified and adopted the
following values;
Transparency and Trust: Open communication, honesty, and reliability in all
planning processes and decision making.
Inclusivity and Respect: Valuing diversity, engaging stakeholders, and respecting
community perspectives.
Shared Purpose and Vision: Craft clear, unified long-term goals that will give
purpose to collaboration, motivating stakeholders to work towards a common
objective and resolve conflicts constructively.
Adaptability and Resilience: Embracing flexibility, learning from experience, and
coping with uncertainty.
Accountability and Responsibility: Taking ownership of planning decisions and
actions.
These values will be foundational to nurturing a collaborative environment where
the district and multiple stakeholders will achieve a unified long-term vision
effectively.

SPATIAL DEVELOPMENT FRAMEWORK
Introduction
The Spatial Development Framework (SDF) guides the district's growth by aligning
future development with its vision, mission, and goals. It optimizes land use,
maximizes infrastructure, protects the environment, and enhances transportation,
settlements, and cultural sites, ensuring sustainable and organized development.
Baseline situation/trends
Chama District has seen substantial changes in recent decades, largely driven by
population growth, which has increased demand for housing and led to a
gradual improvement in building quality. However, many structures remain
substandard, which heightens vulnerability to floods, particularly in areas like
Vilimukulu, Lunzi, Mapamba, Mwalala, Kalinkhu, and Mphalausenga wards.
Water and sanitation have progressed gradually, with population growth straining
both urban and rural water supplies. Partnerships, especially in Chama South,
have been established to enhance water infrastructure, with support from
organizations like World Vision, UNICEF, and TRALARD. Nevertheless, sanitation
remains a critical issue, with only Muchinga Ward declared open-defecation-free
out of 24 wards.
Electricity, primarily supplied by ZESCO, recently improved with the district’s
connection to the national grid in late 2023, leading to infrastructure expansion.
Projects to extend the power distribution to Chikwa, Tembwe, and Kambombo
chiefdoms are underway, alongside a solar project in Lundu. Still, only
Kamphemba Ward has partial access to the national grid.
Forestry resources face pressure due to settlement encroachment in the Lundazi
National Forest. Efforts by the government and partners to promote sustainable
management through community forest areas (CFMAs) are promising, though
challenges remain. A pressing issue is balancing environmental protection with
the demand for resources, such as the government’s goal to provide desks for
students by December 2024, which intensifies forest resource use.
Mining remains largely undeveloped, limited to exploration and small-scale
activities, mainly in the Lundazi forest, adding complexity to conservation efforts.
Tourism continues to be economically important, with community resource
boards (CRBs) funding projects in Lundu, Kambombo, Tembwe, Chikwa, and
Chifunda, although human-wildlife conflicts, particularly during droughts, have
increased in Chama South.
Agriculture has diversified, moving beyond traditional cotton and rice to include
maize, soybeans, and other crops. Livestock farming, predominantly in the North
constituency where wildlife conflicts are minimal, and fish farming are also
developing, though they need further infrastructure and resources.
Population growth has heightened demand for social services, including health,
education, and social welfare. The Constituency Development Fund (CDF) of
2021 has aided in road improvements and educational support, including
secondary school funding and skills training. Social welfare has received boosts in
grants and loans under the new CDF, improving literacy but also leading to an
increase in educated youth seeking employment outside the district.
Commerce and trade have expanded, aided by the CDF, leading to more
cooperatives and economic activities such as small-scale milling, poultry, and
livestock trading. However, growth is limited by a lack of commercial banking
services, with only NATSAVE bank and one official market serving the district.
The ‘Do-Nothing’ Outcomes
Long-term development requires substantial investment, often at a high cost. To
understand if such an investment is essential, here is an analysis of potential
outcomes if current conditions persist.
Firstly, population growth in Chama district is inevitable and central to future
developments. With over 70% of the population relying on subsistence farming,
agriculture is both a critical economic driver and a significant source of
environmental stress. Population growth will increase the demand for food,
leading to a need for more agricultural land and mounting pressure on protected
areas. If left unchecked, this expansion threatens sectors like forestry and energy,
impacting multiple areas.
Population growth also raises the demand for social services. Housing demand is
already high, and without targeted development, the housing shortage will
worsen, bringing additional challenges. Rising demand may attract more real
estate developers but also lead to social and spatial conflicts, including land use
clashes and boundary encroachments. This will further complicate development
across sectors such as water, sanitation, and health.
Similarly, population increases will stress water and sanitation infrastructure.
Without proactive solutions, residents might turn to harmful practices, jeopardizing
the district’s goal of Open Defecation Free (ODF) status. This shift could heighten
exposure to waterborne diseases, especially during rainy seasons or in the event
of flooding.
Increased population will also strain health services and infrastructure, which are
already stretched thin. Accessibility issues, especially due to limited transport
infrastructure, will intensify. The rising demand on healthcare will further stress the
district’s social welfare sector.
A vulnerable, unhealthy society is a poor one, especially since 57% of Chama’s
population is aged 0 to 19 and reliant on a relatively small workforce. Mortality
among the working-age population increases dependency and may push many
young people towards negative coping mechanisms for survival.
Alternative spatial development scenarios
In the following sections, Chama district highlights scenarios deemed to be able
to address the core issues being faced within the district.
First scenario
“A socio-economically sound and sustainable district by 2045”
The first scenario depicted by the district focuses on improving the lives of the
residents through promoting already existing economic activities such as
agriculture and tourism as well as boosting recreational and sporting activities,
sustainable natural resource management, and mining.
Rationale Of Scenario 1
Through this scenario, the district will be able to maximize the received benefits of
its natural resources and sustain them through alternative economic activities that
encourage environmental conservation; activities such as community forest
management areas, carbon harvesting, and beekeeping among others.

Second scenario
“An inter-linked, industrious and sustainable district by 2045”
In this scenario, the district is looking at taking advantage of its geographical
location. Chama is surrounded by five (05) districts and shares a border with
Malawi on the eastern side. Subsequently, the district is a good prospect for the
generation of electrical power through solar power plants.
Rationale Of Scenario 2
By developing the road network, the district can promote economic regional
trade with its neighbors. This in turn will boost industrial activity, hospitality for transit
visitors, and expand the current market for tourism.

Third scenario
“An inclusive, economically stable and sustainable District by 2045”
Like the two scenarios listed above, the third scenario also looks at promoting the
sustainable use of natural resources. However, this scenario takes a step further
by focusing on enhancing the use of water resources.
Rationale Of Scenario 3
Through the development of water harvesting infrastructure in key strategic
positions, the district will boost a number of economic activities within these areas.
Establishing dams and weirs will help transition farmers to improved irrigation
cultivation practices, protect the local scenery for tourism, encourage
industrialization, and mining. This will be topped off by developing an internal road

National forest
Just as is the case of the GMA, a national forest is a creation of the Forestry Act,
2015. While the case of the GMA is meant for the preservation of wildlife, the Forest
Act addresses the protection and preservation of forest areas in the country.
Identification of the areas
As stated earlier, Chama district in located in a game management area and
part of its territory in gazetted as a national forest namely Lundazi National Forest.
The Lundazi National Forest stretches over most of the eastern part of the district
covering a significant area of the Chama South constituency and part of the
eastern territory of the Chama North constituency.
Statement as to the type of development to be permitted
With reference to the Zambia Wildlife Act 2015, settlements, agriculture, and
game ranching are permitted developments within the game management
area. However, activities such as mining are only permitted provided the
prescribed parameters under the Act are observed; These include environmental
protection measures, consent from traditional leadership depending on the land
status, and any other legal prescription that applies within the area in question.

Informal Settlements
As stated earlier in the initial chapters, informal settlements are unplanned
settlements as described under the Urban and Regional Planning Act, 2015. 92%
of Chama district is unplanned with only 8% planned territory in Kamphemba
ward.
Identification of the informal settlements to be upgraded.
Chama District, with 92% of its land unplanned, is prioritizing the Mtayachalo
settlement and planning agreements in two chiefdoms for development
initiatives.
Mtayachalo Area: Located in Kamphemba Ward with 334 households,
Mtayachalo is set for an upgrade to improve public services, including land use
planning, electrification, water, sanitation, and waste management.
Planning Agreements with Chiefs: In line with the Urban and Regional Act of 2015,
the district aims to establish formal agreements with Chief Kambombo in the north
and Chief Chikwa in the south to guide development.
Kaozi Area (Kambombo Chiefdom): Recognized for agricultural growth, Kaozi is
developing an agricultural camp, a livestock dip tank (75% complete), and has
proposals for a health post, primary school, and boarding school, plus 10 hectares
for grazing.
Chikwa Chiefdom: Known for tourism potential, Chikwa features guesthouses,
nine camps, and a safari camp. It’s a primary tourist destination and one of five
proposed sites for a community bush camp.
These efforts aim to drive structured growth, support local economies, and
enhance service provision in the district.

CHAMA TOWN COUNCIL’S FINANCIAL PLAN
Purpose
The aim of this Long-Term Financial Plan is to raise awareness about potential
financial challenges and opportunities that the Council may encounter, guiding
the Institution’s financial and operational decision-makers in preparing for these
possibilities. This five-year financial plan is part of a broader initiative by the
Council to strengthen its long-term financial planning and management
strategies.
Scope
The Council's Financial Plan for Fiscal Years 2025 to 2035 outlines the revenues and
expenditures for all Council funds, including the General Fund and special funds,
over five years.
Description of Development Process
Furthermore, this section of the implementation program describes the policies
and financial abilities to manage the investment needs associated with its spatial
development and built environment through the costing and financing of all
strategies formulated to ensure that the objectives and strategies of the IDP are
well implemented. A capital investment plan would classify specific public
projects as well as a general schedule. The capital Investment Programme is
prepared for five years (2022 to 2026) only and is associated with the Medium-
Term Expenditure Framework, and is directly related to the priorities, objectives
and strategies of the IDP.

The section below provides details of CHAMA Town Council revenue collection
efficiency.
Assessment of Current and Potential Revenue Streams
CHAMA Town Council revenue is low due to low levels of compliancy when it
comes to payments of rates and levies by business owners in the district. Sources
of revenue includes Property Rates, Business Levy, and Grain Levy among many
others.
Own Sources of Revenue (OSR)
A major component of the CHAMA Town Council’s revenue streams includes:
1) Lease and sale of Council land;
2) Property rates and taxes;
3) Business and Personal Levies;
External Sources of Revenues for Implementation
The implementation of CHAMA IDP will mainly depend on funding from the
Government, Donor Agencies, and Private Investors. The council receives
Constituency Development Funds (CDF) for community driven projects, the Local
Government Equalization Fund (LGEF), Grants-in-lieu of rates for implementation
of Capital Projects and Developmental Programmes.
Main Factors affecting Revenue Collection and Management
Main factors affecting revenue collection in the district is lack of transport,
inadequate staff and lack of awareness on the importance of residents and
business owners to pay rates and taxes.

CONCLUSION
Aligned with the Urban and Regional Act of 2015, the Eastern Provincial Planning
Authority, in collaboration with various government bodies, organizations,
stakeholders, and district residents, has completed the Integrated Development
Plan (IDP) for Chama District. This ten-year roadmap reflects a collective and
extensive effort to guide the district's development.
Efforts to create this document began in 2019 but faced numerous setbacks. In
2022, the process gained renewed momentum after the passage of a council
resolution, allowing the district to gather and record key issues from all 24 wards
through thorough public consultations documented in the Planning Survey and
Issues Report (PSIR). This groundwork informed the Development Framework,
which outlined specific interventions to address the district’s challenges. The
framework then underwent a careful review to determine necessary resources,
culminating in the Implementation Plan.
The IDP’s preparation involved significant engagement with residents,
government agencies, line ministries, and non-governmental organizations.
Chama District acknowledges the dedication of all contributors and remains
committed to achieving its vision: “An interlinked, socio-economically sound, and
sustainable district by 2045.”
